stops.label: Ancient sea life
stops.title: It starts with tiny sea life
stops.text: Long ago, tiny sea life called [[plankton]] died and sank into the mud on the seafloor. Over millions of years, layers of mud and sand buried it deeper, and heat and pressure slowly "cooked" it into oil and gas.

terms.plankton: Tiny living things that drift in water, like algae and microscopic animals.

stops.label: Trapped in rock
stops.title: Hiding in rock, like water in a sponge
stops.text: Oil and gas slowly creep upward through the rock until a tight layer of [[cap rock]] stops them, like a lid. Below it, they fill the tiny holes in [[reservoir rock]], like water in a sponge. Everything settles by weight: gas on top, then oil, then salty water.

terms.cap rock: A tight layer of rock that fluids can't pass through. It seals oil and gas in.
terms.reservoir rock: Rock with many tiny connected holes that can hold oil, gas or water.

stops.label: Find & drill
stops.title: Finding it, then drilling down
stops.text: Crews map the rock layers with a [[seismic survey]], which uses sound waves. Then a rig drills down and lines the hole with steel and cement to seal it off from [[groundwater]]. In tight rock, [[fracking]] cracks the rock open so oil and gas can flow out.

terms.seismic survey: Mapping underground rock by sending sound waves down and timing their echoes.
terms.groundwater: Fresh water held in soil and rock near the surface. Many people drink it from wells.
terms.fracking: Short for hydraulic fracturing: pumping water, sand and a little chemical additive into a well at high pressure to crack the rock.

stops.label: Up & split
stops.title: Up the well, then sorted three ways
stops.text: Gas usually rushes up the well on its own, but oil often needs a [[pump jack]] to lift it. What comes up is a mix of gas, oil and salty water, and a [[separator]] lets it settle into layers.
stops.note: This is the fork: gas heads off along the blue route, oil along the amber one.

terms.pump jack: A nodding machine at an oil well. It moves a long rod up and down to lift oil to the surface.
terms.separator: A tank that lets the gas, oil and water coming out of a well separate by weight.

stops.label: Gas plant
stops.title: Cleaning up the gas
stops.text: Raw gas from the well isn't ready to use. A [[processing plant]] dries it, removes impurities, and pulls out heavier gases like propane to sell separately. What's left is the natural gas that heads into the pipelines.

terms.processing plant: A facility that cleans raw natural gas and separates it into useful parts.

stops.label: Pipeline
stops.title: Pushed along long pipelines
stops.text: Clean gas travels long distances through big, buried steel [[pipelines]]. It slowly loses pressure along the way, so [[compressor stations|compressor station]] squeeze it back up to keep it moving.

terms.pipelines: Long steel pipes, usually buried, that carry gas or liquids over long distances.
terms.compressor station: A facility along a pipeline that squeezes the gas to raise its pressure so it keeps flowing.

stops.label: Storage & shipping
stops.title: Saved for winter, or shipped overseas
stops.text: People use far more gas in winter, so extra gas is pumped into [[underground storage]] in warmer months and pulled back out when it's cold. Some gas is chilled until it turns into a liquid, called [[LNG]], so ships can carry it overseas.

terms.underground storage: Places deep underground, like old gas fields or caverns in salt, where gas is kept until it's needed.
terms.LNG: Liquefied natural gas: natural gas chilled until it turns into a liquid, so it takes up far less space.

stops.label: City gate
stops.title: Into town: lower pressure, added smell
stops.text: At the [[city gate]], gas leaves the big pipeline for the local network. Its pressure is lowered, and an [[odorant]] is added, because natural gas has no smell of its own. Smaller pipes under the streets then carry it to a [[gas meter]] at each building.
stops.safety: If you ever smell rotten eggs indoors, leave right away and call the gas company from outside.

terms.city gate: The station where gas moves from a long-distance pipeline into a local delivery network.
terms.odorant: A strong-smelling chemical added to gas so leaks can be noticed.
terms.gas meter: A device on the outside of a building that measures how much gas it uses.

stops.label: Using gas
stops.title: Electricity, heat and things we make
stops.text: Much natural gas goes to [[power plants]] to make electricity. In homes, it fuels furnaces, stoves and water heaters, and factories use it to make things like fertilizer.

terms.power plants: Facilities that make electricity, often by burning fuel to spin a generator.

stops.label: To the refinery
stops.title: Moving crude oil to a refinery
stops.text: [[Crude oil|crude oil]] is the thick, dark oil that comes out of the ground. On land, most of it travels to a [[refinery]] by pipeline. Ships carry it across oceans, and trains and trucks go where there are no pipes.

terms.crude oil: Oil as it comes out of the ground, before a refinery turns it into fuels.

stops.label: Refinery
stops.title: Turning crude oil into fuels
stops.text: At a [[refinery]], crude oil is heated until much of it turns to vapor. In a tall [[distillation tower]], the vapor cools as it rises and turns back to liquid at different heights: gasoline near the top, heavier fuels lower down. The refinery then turns some of the heavier oils into more gasoline and blends the finished fuel.

terms.distillation tower: A tall column where hot vapor cools and turns back to liquid at different heights, sorting crude oil into fuels.

stops.label: Fuel delivery
stops.title: From refinery to your neighborhood
stops.text: Finished fuels travel through pipelines to [[storage terminals]], big tank farms near cities. There, tanker trucks fill up and drive the fuel to gas stations, where it goes into large tanks buried under the station.

terms.storage terminals: Large groups of tanks where fuel is stored and loaded onto trucks.

stops.label: Using gasoline
stops.title: At the pump, then on the road
stops.text: At the station, the pumps draw fuel from the tanks buried below. Most gasoline goes into cars and other vehicles, whose engines burn it to turn the wheels.

glossary.refinery: A plant that turns crude oil into fuels like gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.

overview.title: Two fuels, one beginning
overview.text: Natural gas and gasoline start the same way: tiny sea life, buried and slowly "cooked" by heat and pressure over millions of years into oil and gas. The two often come up the same wells. Then the paths split: gas is cleaned and piped to where it's used, while crude oil goes to a [[refinery]] to become gasoline.

gas.prompt: Natural gas and gasoline both started as…
options: Tiny sea life buried for millions of years
gas.why: Both formed from plankton and algae that were buried and slowly "cooked" by heat and pressure.

gas.prompt: Why does natural gas smell like rotten eggs?
options: A smell is added on purpose so leaks are noticed
It picks up the smell inside pipelines
gas.why: Natural gas has no smell. An odorant is added at the city gate so people can notice a leak.

gas.prompt: What does a compressor station do?
options: Squeezes the gas so it keeps moving down the pipeline
gas.why: Gas loses pressure as it travels. Compressor stations push it back up so it keeps flowing.

options: Soaked into tiny holes in rock
Floating on groundwater near the surface
gasoline.why: Oil fills the tiny spaces in reservoir rock, like water in a sponge, trapped under a cap rock.

options: Pumps oil out of the ground
Turns crude oil into fuels like gasoline
Adds a smell to natural gas
gasoline.why: A refinery heats and separates crude oil, then turns it into finished fuels like gasoline.

gasoline.prompt: Where is the fuel kept at a gas station?
options: In large tanks buried under the station
In tanker trucks parked out back
gasoline.why: Tanker trucks unload into large tanks buried under the station, and the pumps draw fuel from them.

timelapse.caption: Plankton thrive in a warm, shallow sea. When they die, they sink into the mud.
Low oxygen on the seafloor stops them rotting away. A dark, rich mud builds up.
Rivers dump sand and mud on top. Layer by layer, the remains are buried deeper.
Now buried deep, where it is hot, the remains slowly turn into oil.
Deeper, hotter parts turn into gas. Oil and gas creep upward through the rock.
They collect in porous sandstone, trapped under tight cap rock. Today, we drill for them.
